content:
Quick answer: You may get a Blue Badge if arthritis makes walking very difficult because of pain, the time it takes or the risk of falling. Some people qualify automatically, for example with 8 points or more in the PIP or ADP 'moving around' activity. Otherwise your council assesses you. Apply through GOV.UK in England, Scotland and Wales, or nidirect in Northern Ireland.

Checked on 10 October 2026 against GOV.UK: Apply for or renew a Blue Badge, the GOV.UK England eligibility guidance, mygov.scot, GOV.WALES and nidirect. Councils run the scheme locally, so check your own council's website as well.

When arthritis in your hips, knees, feet or spine makes every walk across a car park a calculation, a Blue Badge can make a big difference. It lets you park closer to where you are going, so you can save your energy for the shopping, appointment or visit itself. This matters even more if you are also becoming frailer, are unsteady on your feet or have had falls. This guide explains who qualifies, how to describe your walking accurately, and how the scheme differs across the UK.

What a Blue Badge is

  • A parking permit for people with severe mobility problems, whether they drive or are a passenger.
  • It belongs to you, not to a car. Anyone driving you can use it, but only when you are travelling with them (or they are collecting or dropping you off where the rules allow).
  • GOV.UK says badges usually last up to 3 years. You must reapply before your badge expires; it does not renew automatically.
  • It is issued by your local council (in Northern Ireland, by the Blue Badge Unit through nidirect).

Two routes: automatic and assessed

There are two ways to qualify. Some people are eligible "automatically" (without further assessment) because of a benefit they get. Everyone else can still apply, and the council assesses whether their walking is affected enough.

Automatic eligibility through benefits

NationAutomatic routes most relevant to arthritis
EnglandPIP with 8 points or more in the "moving around" activity; higher rate mobility component of DLA. For "planning and following journeys", only 10 points for descriptor E (overwhelming psychological distress) is automatic
ScotlandAdult Disability Payment with 8 points or more in "moving around" or 12 points in "planning and following a journey"; enhanced mobility under special rules for terminal illness; higher rate mobility of Scottish Adult DLA
WalesPIP with 8 points or more for moving around, or 12 points for planning and following a journey; higher rate mobility component of DLA
Northern IrelandPIP with 8 points or more in "moving around"; higher rate mobility component of DLA

Each nation also lists other automatic routes, such as War Pensioners' Mobility Supplement, certain Armed Forces Compensation Scheme awards and being registered blind or severely sight impaired. Check the official page for your nation, linked in the sources.

If you get PIP, you will need your award letter showing the mobility scores. The England guidance asks for the pages that show your entitlement and your mobility scores.

The assessed route

If you do not get a qualifying benefit, or your PIP points are lower, you can still apply. The England guidance says you may be eligible if, for example:

  • you cannot walk at all
  • you cannot walk without help from someone else or using mobility aids
  • you find walking very difficult due to pain, breathlessness or the time it takes
  • walking is dangerous to your health and safety
  • you have a severe disability in both arms and drive regularly, but cannot operate pay-and-display machines

The other nations use similar criteria. People with arthritis most often apply because walking is very painful, very slow or unsafe. Badges can also be issued for some non-visible (hidden) conditions that make journeys very difficult.

How to describe your walking honestly and accurately

The council needs to understand what walking is really like for you. Vague answers such as "I struggle to walk" are hard to assess. Before you apply:

  1. Measure a familiar route. Use a map app to measure, say, your front door to the post box. Then you can say "about 40 metres" with confidence.
  2. Time it. How long does that distance take you compared with before your arthritis?
  3. Note when pain starts and when you have to stop. Many people can keep going after pain begins, but much more slowly. Say so.
  4. Describe what you use: a stick, crutches, a frame, a rollator, a wheelchair or someone's arm.
  5. Describe the effect afterwards: how long you need to rest and whether it affects the rest of your day or the next day.
  6. Include falls and near misses, and anything that makes you unsafe, such as knees giving way, dizziness or poor balance.
  7. Think about your usual day, not your best. If it varies, explain how often you have bad days.

A walking log over a week or two can help. Our free evidence diary templates include one you can print.

If you are also becoming frail

Arthritis and frailty often overlap in later life. Weakness, low stamina, fear of falling and slower walking can all add to joint pain. Describe the whole picture: for example, "my knees hurt after a few steps, my legs feel weak and I have fallen twice this year". If you use a walking aid because you are unsteady, say so, and mention any falls clinic, physiotherapy or occupational therapy input.

Supporting evidence

  • Clinic letters that describe your walking, falls or mobility, not only the diagnosis
  • Physiotherapy or occupational therapy reports
  • A list of your medicines and walking aids
  • Your PIP or ADP award letter showing points, even if not enough for automatic eligibility

The council may ask for more information or invite you to a mobility assessment with an independent professional.

How to apply

  • England, Scotland and Wales: apply online through GOV.UK, which sends your application to your council, or contact your council directly. Wales also lets you apply through your local authority.
  • Northern Ireland: apply online or by post through nidirect; the Blue Badge Unit processes applications.

GOV.UK says you will need a recent digital photo of your head and shoulders, and a photo or scan of proof of identity, proof of address and proof of benefits if you get any. You will also need your National Insurance number if you have one. You can save your application and come back to it.

Costs and how long it takes

NationCostDecision time (official guidance)
EnglandUp to £10Usually within 12 weeks
ScotlandUp to £20 (most councils charge £20)Reapply at least 12 weeks before expiry
WalesFreeSet by your local authority
Northern Ireland£10 (refunded if unsuccessful)See nidirect

Only apply through official sites. GOV.WALES warns that websites charging you to apply are not genuine providers.

If your application is refused

GOV.UK says your council should tell you why. You can ask them to reconsider if you think important information was not taken into account. You can also reapply if your mobility gets worse. When asking for a reconsideration, explain what was missed, add any new evidence (such as a walking log or a recent physio letter), and be specific about distance, time, pain and safety.

Using your badge: the main rules

In England, the official rights and responsibilities guidance says:

  • Yellow lines: badge holders may park on single or double yellow lines for up to 3 hours, but generally not where there are loading or unloading restrictions. You must display the badge and the blue parking clock.
  • On-street meters and pay-and-display: you may usually park free, and without a time limit unless signs say otherwise.
  • Disabled bays on the street: usually free, and without a time limit unless signs show one.
  • Off-street car parks (supermarkets, hospitals, council car parks): it is up to the owner whether badge holders park free. Check the signs.
  • Central London: parts of central London have their own schemes, so check the local rules.

Rules are broadly similar but not identical in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland. Your badge pack explains the rules where you live. Misusing a badge is a criminal offence; in England the guidance says it could lead to a fine of up to £1,000. Return the badge if you no longer need it.

Other help with getting around

  • The Motability Scheme if you get the higher rate of the PIP mobility part. See our Motability guide.
  • A Disabled Persons Railcard if you get either part of PIP, and local bus travel concessions from your council.
  • Your council may be able to provide a disabled parking bay outside your home, depending on local rules.
  • Getting the right walking aid and footwear can help you walk further more safely. Ask your GP, physiotherapist or podiatrist.

Living in Scotland? Our Scotland Blue Badge guide covers the Scottish process in more detail. For how the PIP "moving around" activity is scored, see our complete PIP guide.

Free help with an application

Your council's Blue Badge team can answer questions about the process. For independent help, Citizens Advice, Citizens Advice Scotland, Advice NI, Scope and Disability Rights UK provide free information. We are not connected to these organisations.

When to get medical help

If walking has become much harder recently, do not just apply for a badge; see your GP or physiotherapist too, as there may be treatment, aids or exercise that help. Get urgent advice from NHS 111 or your GP if a joint suddenly becomes hot, swollen and very painful, especially with fever, or if you cannot bear weight after a fall. Call 999 if you have a fall with a head injury, severe pain or cannot get up.

Frequently asked questions

Can I get a Blue Badge for arthritis?

Yes, if arthritis makes walking very difficult because of pain, the time it takes or the risk to your safety, or if you get a qualifying benefit such as PIP with 8 or more points in moving around. The diagnosis alone is not enough.

Do I need PIP to get a Blue Badge?

No. PIP or ADP can make you eligible automatically, but you can apply without them and the council will assess your mobility.

How much does a Blue Badge cost?

Up to £10 in England, up to £20 in Scotland, free in Wales and £10 in Northern Ireland, according to the official guidance checked on 10 October 2026.

How long does a Blue Badge last?

Usually up to 3 years. It does not renew automatically, so reapply before it expires. In Scotland, mygov.scot advises reapplying at least 12 weeks before.

Can someone else use my Blue Badge?

Only when they are driving you. Using it when you are not travelling is misuse and can lead to a fine.

What if I am refused?

Ask the council to reconsider, explaining what was missed and adding new evidence. You can also reapply if your mobility gets worse.
